events.title: Themistius' oration on religious toleration
events.summary: On 1 January 364, at Jovian's consular inauguration in Ancyra, the pagan philosopher-senator Themistius delivered Oration 5, praising Jovian's law granting freedom of worship and arguing that God delights in diversity of worship, as the constitution of the universe delights in variety.

events.title: Valentinian bans nocturnal sacrifices; Praetextatus' plea
events.summary: A law of September 364 (CTh 9.16.7) banned nocturnal sacrifices and magical rites; Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, proconsul of Achaea, persuaded Valentinian to exempt the Eleusinian Mysteries, telling him that life would be unlivable for the Greeks without them.

events.title: Alamanni cross the frozen Rhine
events.summary: Insulted by meagre gifts from Valentinian's master of offices Ursatius, the Alamanni broke across the Rhine in January 365 and defeated the comites Charietto and Severianus; Valentinian, on his way to the Rhine, heard of Procopius' revolt the same autumn but chose to stay in Gaul.

events.title: Jovinus defeats the Alamanni at Scarponna and Catalauni
events.summary: The magister equitum Jovinus surprised one Alamannic band bathing and drinking at Scarponna on the Moselle, another at a river crossing, and then defeated the main force near Catalauni (Châlons), where Ammianus reports 6,000 Alamanni killed and 4,000 wounded against 1,200 Roman dead.

events.title: Fifth exile of Athanasius
events.summary: Valens' order of May 365 that bishops exiled by Constantius and restored by Julian should leave again led to riots; Athanasius withdrew on 5 October 365 to a family tomb outside the city for four months, until the emperor, alarmed by Procopius, allowed him back on 1 February 366.

events.title: Gold refining and the OB mark
events.summary: Between 366 and 368 Valentinian and Valens ordered all gold received in taxes to be melted into bullion and that solidi be struck only at the court (comitatus), adding OB (obryzum, refined gold; also the Greek numeral 72) to the mintmark; the purity of the solidus rose to about 99%. Laws of the same years tie this to the comes sacrarum largitionum.
scholarship: Hendy, Studies in the Byzantine Monetary Economy (1985)

events.title: Alamanni sack Mogontiacum at Easter
events.summary: The Alamannic prince Rando slipped into undefended Mainz during a Christian festival, probably Easter 368, and carried off men and women of every rank with their possessions; Valentinian responded with the campaign that ended at Solicinium.

events.title: Valentinian's Rhine and Danube fortification programme
events.summary: From 369 Valentinian fortified the Rhine from Raetia to the North Sea with new forts, watchtowers (burgi) and landing places on the far bank (e.g. Altrip, Mannheim-Neckarau, Engers), and diverted the Neckar to protect a fort; Ammianus also describes a fort at Mons Piri destroyed by Alamanni while under construction. Many Danube burgi date from the same years.

events.title: Conspiracy of Valentinus in Britain
events.summary: Valentinus, a Pannonian exiled to Britain for a serious crime and the brother-in-law of the notorious prefect Maximinus, plotted with exiles and soldiers to seize power during Count Theodosius' restoration of the province; Theodosius had him and his closest associates executed but forbade further inquiries.

events.title: Saxon raiders massacred after a truce
events.summary: A Saxon war band that had raided along the coast to the Rhine was defeated by Severus, magister peditum, and granted safe passage in return for recruits; Roman troops then ambushed and annihilated them. Ammianus admits the treachery but calls it just; Jerome locates a Saxon defeat at Deuso.

events.title: Basil becomes bishop of Caesarea; the Basileias
events.summary: Basil, who had founded ascetic communities in Pontus and written the "Longer Rules", became bishop of Caesarea in 370 and built outside the city a complex of hospital, poorhouse, hostel and workshops, the Basileias, admired by Gregory of Nazianzus as a "new city". He stood up to Valens' prefect Modestus, who said no one had ever spoken to him so boldly.

events.title: Siege of Artogerassa; Queen Pharantzem's defence
events.summary: After Shapur II seized King Arsaces (Arshak) II by treachery, the queen Pharantzem held out in the fortress of Artogerassa with Arsaces' treasure for over a year, while their son Pap escaped to the Romans; the fortress eventually fell and the queen was taken to Persia and killed.

battle.significance: Demonstrated the collapse of Roman influence in Armenia after 363.

events.debate: Date 368-370; Faustus and Ammianus differ on details.

events.title: Battle of Bagavan
events.summary: Roman troops under Traianus and Vadomarius, sent to support King Pap, together with the Armenian sparapet Mushegh, defeated a Persian army at Bagavan; a truce followed, with Shapur refusing to recognise Roman influence in Armenia and Iberia divided between rival kings.

events.title: Martin becomes bishop of Tours
events.summary: Martin, a Pannonian ex-soldier who had founded the first Gallic monastery at Ligugé c. 361, was acclaimed bishop of Tours on 4 July 371 (or 372) despite opposition from bishops who disliked his shabby appearance; he founded Marmoutier across the Loire and campaigned against rural shrines, as told in Sulpicius Severus' Life.

events.title: Ausonius writes the Mosella
events.summary: Ausonius, rhetor of Bordeaux and tutor of Gratian at the court of Trier, composed the Mosella, 483 hexameters on a journey down the Moselle from Bingen, celebrating its villas, vineyard-clad slopes and fishes (some 15 species named); it is the finest poem of fourth-century Gaul and an early witness to Moselle viticulture.

events.title: Death of Athanasius
events.summary: Athanasius died in Alexandria on 2 May 373, having designated his brother Peter as successor; Valens' prefect Palladius immediately installed the Arian Lucius with violence, and Peter fled to Rome.

events.title: Valentinian's treaty with Macrianus on the Rhine
events.summary: After failing to kidnap him in 372, Valentinian met the Bucinobantian king Macrianus in boats on the Rhine near Mainz and made a treaty; Macrianus remained loyal until killed fighting the Franks.

events.title: Quadi and Sarmatians invade Pannonia
events.summary: The murder of the Quadic king Gabinius at a banquet by the dux Marcellianus provoked a Quadic and Sarmatian invasion that caught the princess Constantia (Gratian's bride) at a villa near Sirmium, nearly captured her, and destroyed two legions; the young Theodosius, dux of Moesia, defeated the Sarmatians.

events.title: Romans murder King Pap of Armenia
events.summary: Suspecting Pap of dealing with Persia, Valens had the dux Traianus invite him to a banquet where he was murdered (374 or 375); Ammianus condemns the treachery, recalling the precedent of Fabricius who refused to murder Pyrrhus.

events.title: Valentinian II proclaimed at Aquincum
events.summary: Six days after Valentinian I's death, the generals Merobaudes and Equitius had his four-year-old son by Justina proclaimed Augustus at Aquincum on 22 November 375 without consulting Gratian or Valens, who accepted the fait accompli.

events.title: Execution of Count Theodosius at Carthage
events.summary: Early in 376, after suppressing Firmus, the magister equitum Theodosius was beheaded at Carthage in obscure circumstances, probably a victim of court factions after Valentinian's death; he was baptised beforehand. His son retired to Spain until recalled in 378.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

events.title: Revolt of Queen Mavia's Saracens
events.summary: After her husband's death the Saracen queen Mavia led her people (probably Tanukh) against Roman Arabia, Palestine and Phoenicia, defeating Roman forces; she made peace on condition that the hermit Moses be consecrated bishop for her people, and gave her daughter in marriage to the magister Victor. Her cavalry served Valens in 378.

events.title: Massacre of Gothic youths in the east
events.summary: After Adrianople the magister Julius, fearing a rising, had Gothic youths and hostages who had been distributed among eastern cities gathered on a fixed day on pretext of pay and massacred.

events.title: The Gothic attack on Constantinople and the Saracen sortie
events.summary: After Adrianople the Goths advanced on Constantinople but were repulsed by a sortie of Mavia's Saracen cavalry; Ammianus describes a long-haired Saracen, naked but for a loincloth, cutting a Goth's throat and drinking his blood, which terrified the Goths into withdrawing. The widow Domnica paid volunteers.

battle.significance: Saved the capital; the Goths turned back to the Balkans.

events.title: Gregory of Nazianzus leads the Nicenes of Constantinople
events.summary: Invited by the small Nicene congregation, Gregory preached in a private house chapel, the Anastasia, from 379, delivering the five Theological Orations (27-31) in 380; on 27 November 380 Theodosius expelled the Homoian bishop Demophilus and led Gregory into the Holy Apostles under military guard.

events.title: Theodosius defeated by the Goths in Macedonia
events.summary: In 380 Theodosius, campaigning with an army padded out with Gothic recruits, was routed in Macedonia when barbarians in his own ranks went over to Fritigern; he fell ill at Thessalonica, was baptised by Acholius, and left the war to Gratian's generals Bauto and Arbogast.

battle.significance: Confirmed that the Goths could not be destroyed militarily, leading to the 382 treaty.

events.title: Athanaric received at Constantinople
events.summary: Expelled by his own people, the Tervingian judge Athanaric, who had sworn never to set foot on Roman soil, arrived in Constantinople on 11 January 381; Theodosius met him outside the city, and when he died two weeks later (25 January) gave him a magnificent funeral. His followers entered Roman service.

events.title: Council of Aquileia
events.summary: Ambrose presided over a western council at Aquileia on 3 September 381 that condemned the Homoian bishops Palladius of Ratiaria and Secundianus of Singidunum; the stenographic minutes survive, with Palladius' Arian rebuttal in the margins of a Paris manuscript.

events.title: Gratian removes the Altar of Victory and disendows the cults
events.summary: Gratian ordered the Altar of Victory removed from the Senate house again, confiscated the endowments of the Vestals and priestly colleges, and abolished their immunities; a senatorial embassy under Symmachus was refused an audience at Pope Damasus' instigation.

events.title: Gratian gives up the title pontifex maximus
events.summary: Zosimus tells how Gratian refused the robe of pontifex maximus offered by the pontiffs, one of whom remarked that "if the emperor will not be pontifex, Maximus will soon be pontifex", foreshadowing Magnus Maximus. Inscriptions show Gratian with the title until about 379-382.
events.debate: Date 379, 382 or 383; Alan Cameron argues the title was dropped in 379 and the story is unhistorical.

events.title: Jerome in Rome begins revising the Latin Bible
events.summary: As secretary to Damasus from 382, Jerome revised the Old Latin Gospels against the Greek, completed by 384, and gathered a circle of ascetic aristocratic women on the Aventine (Marcella, Paula, Eustochium). Forced out of Rome in 385, he settled at Bethlehem (386) and translated the Old Testament from Hebrew (390-405), producing the core of the Vulgate.

events.title: Arcadius proclaimed Augustus
events.summary: On 19 January 383, at the Hebdomon parade ground, Theodosius raised his six-year-old elder son Arcadius to Augustus, establishing a dynasty that would rule the east until 450.

events.title: Egeria's pilgrimage
events.summary: Between about 381 and 384 Egeria, a well-born woman probably from Gallaecia, travelled to Sinai, Egypt, Jerusalem, Mount Nebo, Edessa and Carrhae, writing letters to her "sisters" at home. Her surviving account describes the liturgy of Jerusalem in detail, including Holy Week, Palm Sunday and the veneration of the cross.
events.debate: Dates 381-384 are accepted by most; her origin from Gallaecia rests on a seventh-century letter of Valerius of Bierzo.

events.title: Maternus Cynegius and the destruction of eastern temples
events.summary: The praetorian prefect Maternus Cynegius, a pious Spaniard, toured Egypt and the east from 384 to 388 closing temples; at Apamea Bishop Marcellus demolished the great temple of Zeus with soldiers and a fire under its columns, and was later killed by pagans while destroying a shrine near Aulon. Libanius' Oration 30, "For the Temples", protests against black-robed monks wrecking rural shrines.
events.debate: How far Cynegius acted on imperial orders rather than his own zeal is debated (Fowden).

events.title: Conversion of Augustine at Milan
events.summary: In August 386 Augustine, imperial professor of rhetoric at Milan, after reading Neoplatonist books (Plotinus and Porphyry in Victorinus' Latin), hearing Ambrose preach and the story of Antony, heard a child chanting "tolle lege" and opened Paul's letter to the Romans; he resigned, retired to Cassiciacum, and was baptised by Ambrose at Easter (24-25 April) 387.

events.title: Promotus destroys the Greuthungi of Odotheus on the Danube
events.summary: When the Greuthungian chieftain Odotheus tried to cross the Danube with a large following in dugout canoes, the magister Promotus, having lured them with false deserters, met them midstream with warships and slaughtered them; survivors were settled in Phrygia. Claudian later celebrated the victory.

battle.significance: Prevented a second mass crossing of the Danube.

sources.w: Panegyric on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius

events.title: Magnus Maximus invades Italy
events.summary: Exploiting a mission by Domninus to obtain troops, Maximus crossed the Alps behind the envoys in late summer 387; Valentinian II and Justina fled by sea from Aquileia to Thessalonica, where Theodosius married Valentinian's sister Galla and agreed to war.

events.title: Theodosius in Rome
events.summary: Theodosius entered Rome on 13 June 389 with his son Honorius and Valentinian II, celebrating a triumph over Maximus; he showed courtesy to the Senate and Pacatus Drepanius delivered his panegyric. Symmachus, who had praised Maximus, had to seek pardon in a speech of apology.

events.title: Frankish invasion and the disaster in the Silva Carbonaria
events.summary: While Maximus fought in Italy, Franks under Genobaudes, Marcomer and Sunno raided Germania Secunda; the Roman commander Quintinus pursued them across the Rhine and was ambushed among swamps and forest, losing most of his army. The account survives from Sulpicius Alexander via Gregory of Tours.
events.locName: Germania Secunda and the Silva Carbonaria

battle.significance: Exposed the Lower Rhine and led to Arbogast's punitive campaigns.

events.title: Theodosius bans all pagan cult
events.summary: A law of 8 November 392 to the prefect Rufinus (CTh 16.10.12) banned sacrifice and divination under penalty of treason and forbade even private worship of the lares with fire, the genius with wine or the penates with incense, garlands or lamps, with fines for decurions who failed to enforce it; it is often treated as the formal end of legal paganism.
events.debate: Enforcement was patchy; temples and private cult continued in many places into the sixth century.

events.title: Synod of Hippo and the African canon of Scripture
events.summary: A plenary African council at Hippo on 8 October 393, at which the priest Augustine preached De fide et symbolo, listed the canonical books of the Bible, including the deuterocanonical books; the list was reaffirmed at Carthage in 397.

events.title: Honorius proclaimed Augustus
events.summary: On 23 January 393, in answer to Eugenius' proclamation, Theodosius made his eight-year-old younger son Honorius Augustus at the Hebdomon, signalling that he would not accept Arbogast's emperor.

events.title: The pagan revival under Eugenius and Flavianus
events.summary: Under Eugenius, a Christian rhetor dependent on Arbogast, the praetorian prefect Virius Nicomachus Flavianus celebrated festivals, purified the city, restored the temple of Venus at Rome and set up statues of Jupiter and a Hercules banner for the army at the Frigidus. The anonymous Carmen contra paganos may attack him; after the Frigidus Flavianus committed suicide.
events.debate: Alan Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011), argues the "pagan revival" has been exaggerated by Christian sources and modern romanticism.

events.title: The last dated hieroglyphic inscription
events.summary: On 24 August 394, the birthday of Osiris, a priest named Esmet-Akhom carved a figure of the god Mandulis with a hieroglyphic text in the Gate of Hadrian at Philae, the last known hieroglyphic inscription; the last demotic graffito there dates to 452. The temple served the Blemmyes and Nobades until closed under Justinian.

events.title: Rebuilding of St Paul's Outside the Walls
events.summary: Valentinian II, Theodosius and Arcadius wrote to the prefect of Rome Sallustius in 384-386 ordering a great new basilica over Paul's tomb on the Via Ostiensis, replacing the small Constantinian church; the five-aisled building, finished under Honorius, rivalled St Peter's until it burned in 1823.

events.title: Successive reductions of the nummus (follis)
events.summary: Diocletian's silver-washed nummus of c. 10 g (1/32 pound) was cut to about 1/40 pound in 307, 1/48 in 310, 1/72 by 313 and about 3 g (1/96) by 318, while its silver wash shrank; prices in papyri rise accordingly. These cuts were made at different moments by rival emperors, creating regional differences.

events.title: GLORIA EXERCITVS and the small Constantinian nummus
events.summary: From 330 all mints struck a light nummus (c. 2.5 g, later c. 1.7 g from 335) with two soldiers and two standards (later one) and the legend GLORIA EXERCITVS, alongside URBS ROMA and CONSTANTINOPOLIS commemorative types; these are among the commonest ancient coins found today.

events.title: Introduction of the siliqua and miliarense
events.summary: Constantine introduced new silver denominations in the 320s, the miliarense (1/72 and 1/60 pound) and later the siliqua (1/96 pound), named for the carob seed (1/24 solidus); they served largely as donatives to the army and court rather than everyday money.
events.debate: Names attested later; how they were tariffed against the solidus is debated.

events.title: Laws against melting and trading coin
events.summary: Laws of the 350s (CTh 9.23.1, 356) forbade merchants to carry more than 1,000 folles for trade and banned melting down or separating silver from the large bronze (maiorina), which was demonetised; the hoarding of the larger pieces shows public distrust of the coinage.

events.title: Julian's bull coinage
events.summary: Julian issued a large bronze coin with a bull and two stars and the legend SECURITAS REIPUB; Christians mocked it as an emblem of his sacrifices, though it may represent Apis or his zodiac sign. His bearded philosopher portrait broke with the clean-shaven Constantinian image and was mocked by the Antiochenes.
events.debate: Meaning of the bull disputed: Apis, the bull of Mithras, Julian's horoscope (Taurus) or sacrifice.

events.title: Plotinus founds his school in Rome
events.summary: After eleven years with Ammonius Saccas at Alexandria and joining Gordian III's Persian expedition to learn Persian and Indian philosophy, Plotinus settled in Rome in 244 and taught in the house of the widow Gemina; his circle included senators such as Rogatianus, who gave up his property, the physician Eustochius, Amelius and, from 263, Porphyry. He began writing only in 253-254.

events.title: Porphyry writes Against the Christians
events.summary: Porphyry composed fifteen books against the Christians, using historical criticism to date Daniel to the Maccabean era and exposing contradictions in the Gospels; it was answered by Methodius, Eusebius and Apollinaris and burned by order of Constantine and again of Theodosius II and Valentinian III in 448. Only fragments survive.
events.debate: Date c. 270-300; whether the fragments of Macarius Magnes' pagan are Porphyry is disputed.

events.title: Porphyry publishes the Enneads
events.summary: About 301, some thirty years after Plotinus' death, Porphyry arranged his master's 54 treatises into six groups of nine (Enneads), prefacing them with the Life of Plotinus; his Isagoge, an introduction to Aristotle's Categories, became the most-read logic textbook of the Middle Ages.

events.title: Iamblichus' school at Apamea
events.summary: Iamblichus of Chalcis, Porphyry's pupil and critic, taught at Apamea from about 305 a Neoplatonism centred on theurgy, ritual that united the soul with the gods; his pupils Aedesius, Sopater and the Maximus who taught Julian made his system the philosophy of the late pagan revival.

events.title: Lactantius writes the Divine Institutes
events.summary: Lactantius, an African rhetor appointed to teach Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia by Diocletian and dismissed in the persecution, wrote seven books of Divine Institutes (c. 303-310), the first systematic Latin exposition of Christianity, aimed at educated pagans; later he tutored Crispus in Trier and wrote De Mortibus Persecutorum (c. 314-315).

events.title: Eusebius publishes the Ecclesiastical History
events.summary: Eusebius of Caesarea, pupil of Pamphilus and heir to Origen's library, published the first church history in successive editions (books 1-7 perhaps before 303; books 8-10 added 313-325), quoting hundreds of documents; with his Chronicle, which tabulated sacred and secular chronology in parallel columns, it created the framework of Christian historiography.
events.debate: Number and dates of editions (Schwartz, Barnes, Burgess) disputed.

events.title: Arnobius writes Against the Pagans
events.summary: Arnobius, a rhetor at Sicca Veneria and teacher of Lactantius, wrote seven books Adversus Nationes around 300 to prove the sincerity of his conversion to his bishop; they are a mine of information on the pagan cults they ridicule.

events.title: Juvencus versifies the Gospels
events.summary: The Spanish priest Gaius Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus composed the Evangeliorum libri IV, a Virgilian hexameter harmony of the Gospels of some 3,200 lines, around 329; it is the first Christian Latin epic and was a school text through the Middle Ages.

events.title: Optatianus Porfyrius' figured poems for Constantine
events.summary: Publilius Optatianus Porfyrius, exiled under unclear circumstances, won his recall and later the urban prefecture by sending Constantine a book of carmina cancellata: grids of letters in which coloured verses form chi-rhos, palm branches, a ship and other images inside the poem.
events.debate: Dates of the collection (c. 324-326) and exile debated.

events.title: Firmicus Maternus urges the destruction of paganism
events.summary: Julius Firmicus Maternus, a Sicilian senator who had written the Mathesis, the most complete Latin astrological handbook (c. 335), converted and addressed to Constantius and Constans On the Error of Profane Religions (c. 346), urging them to stamp out pagan cults by force and providing unique detail on mystery rituals.

events.title: Aurelius Victor writes De Caesaribus
events.summary: Sextus Aurelius Victor, a self-made African of humble birth, finished his short imperial history from Augustus to 360 in 361; Julian, meeting him at Sirmium, made him consular of Pannonia Secunda and honoured him with a bronze statue, and he later served as prefect of Rome (389).

events.title: Eutropius dedicates his Breviarium to Valens
events.summary: Eutropius, magister memoriae, wrote a ten-book summary of Roman history from Romulus to Jovian for Valens in about 369, as Festus did shortly after, to prepare the emperor for war with Persia; it was translated into Greek within a generation and became a school book for over a millennium.

events.title: Libanius writes his autobiography
events.summary: Libanius, official sophist of Antioch, composed the first part of his Autobiography (Oration 1) in 374, extending it until 393; with 64 orations and about 1,500 letters it gives the most intimate surviving view of a late antique city, its council, schools and quarrels.

events.title: Proba composes her Virgilian cento
events.summary: Faltonia Betitia Proba, a Christian aristocrat of the Anician circle, retold the Creation and the life of Christ in 694 lines stitched together entirely from Virgil (Cento Vergilianus de laudibus Christi), the first substantial surviving work by a Christian Latin woman poet; Jerome disliked it, but it was widely copied.
events.debate: Date c. 352-384; most place it in the 360s, possibly in response to Julian's school law.

events.title: De Rebus Bellicis
events.summary: An anonymous treatise addressed to emperors (probably Valentinian and Valens, c. 368-369) proposes reforms of coinage, taxation and the army along with illustrated war machines, including an ox-powered paddle-wheel warship and a mobile bridge on inflated skins; it diagnoses gold hoarding by the rich as the root of the empire's troubles.
events.debate: Date disputed (337-400); Valentinian-Valens most widely accepted.

events.title: Villa del Casale at Piazza Armerina
events.summary: A vast late Roman villa built c. 310-340 with some 3,500 m² of mosaics, including a 60 m corridor of the Great Hunt showing animals captured in Africa and India for the games, and the "bikini girls" exercising; its owner was an imperial-level senator, perhaps a Ceionius or Maximian himself.
events.debate: Ownership hotly debated (Maximian, a Nicomachus, Proculus Populonius or other senator).

events.title: Galerius builds Felix Romuliana
events.summary: Galerius built a fortified palace at his birthplace, naming it after his mother Romula, with temples, baths and on the nearby hill of Magura the mausolea and consecration mounds of Romula and Galerius himself, who was buried there in 311. An archivolt inscribed FELIX ROMULIANA confirmed the identification in 1984.

events.title: Maxentius' villa, circus and mausoleum on the Via Appia
events.summary: Maxentius built a palace complex at the third mile of the Via Appia with a circus 513 m long, its spina adorned with the obelisk now in Piazza Navona, and a rotunda mausoleum where his son Valerius Romulus (d. 309) was buried; he also restored the Temple of Venus and Roma after a fire and began the Basilica Nova.

events.title: Funerary basilica of Sant'Agnese and the mausoleum of Constantina
events.summary: Constantine's daughter Constantina built a huge U-shaped funerary basilica beside Agnes' tomb, one of a series of circus-shaped cemetery basilicas (San Lorenzo, Santi Marcellino e Pietro with Helena's mausoleum, San Sebastiano); her domed mausoleum, now Santa Costanza, keeps vault mosaics of vintage scenes with putti treading grapes.
events.debate: Dates c. 337-351.

events.title: Damasus restores the martyrs' tombs
events.summary: Pope Damasus I monumentalised the tombs of Roman martyrs with verse epitaphs carved by the calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus in a distinctive lettering (the Filocalian script), turning the catacombs into pilgrimage shrines and promoting Rome's apostolic and martyr prestige; his inscription for the Crypt of the Popes survives in Callixtus.

events.title: Melania the Elder and Rufinus found monasteries on the Mount of Olives
events.summary: The Roman aristocrat Melania the Elder, widowed at 22, after visiting the Egyptian monks founded a convent on the Mount of Olives (c. 378-380), while Rufinus of Aquileia founded a men's monastery nearby; their hospitality made Jerusalem a centre of Latin asceticism, and Rufinus later translated Origen and Eusebius.
events.debate: Founding date c. 378-381.

events.title: Evagrius Ponticus withdraws to Nitria and the Kellia
events.summary: Evagrius, a deacon ordained by Gregory of Nazianzus who fled Constantinople after an affair, settled in Nitria and then the Kellia in 383, where he wrote the Praktikos and the theory of eight evil thoughts (logismoi) that became, via Cassian and Gregory the Great, the seven deadly sins.

events.title: Hilarion introduces monasticism to Palestine
events.summary: According to Jerome's Life, Hilarion of Thabatha, who had studied at Alexandria and visited Antony, settled as a hermit near Gaza around 306-308 and attracted disciples, the first monastic movement in Palestine; Sozomen, from the region, confirms his fame.
events.debate: Jerome's Life is partly romance; dates approximate.

events.title: Hilary of Poitiers exiled to Phrygia
events.summary: Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, condemned at the synod of Béziers in 356 for opposing Saturninus of Arles, was exiled to Phrygia, where he learned eastern theology and wrote De Trinitate and De Synodis, explaining the eastern homoiousians to the west; he returned in 360-361 and became the leading anti-Arian in Gaul.

events.title: Basil and Gregory compile the Philocalia of Origen at Annesi
events.summary: Basil, after visiting the monks of Egypt and Syria, retired with his family's ascetic household at Annesi (led by his sister Macrina) and was joined by Gregory of Nazianzus; they compiled the Philocalia, an anthology of Origen's writings, and the Moralia, laying the foundations of Byzantine monasticism.
events.debate: Attribution of the Philocalia to them is traditional.

events.title: Ulfilas translates the Bible into Gothic
events.summary: After leading his persecuted Gothic Christians into Moesia (c. 348), Ulfilas invented a Gothic alphabet from Greek, Latin and runic letters and translated the Bible, leaving out the Books of Kings to avoid encouraging the warlike Goths (Philostorgius). The Codex Argenteus in Uppsala preserves much of the Gospels.

events.title: Athanaric's persecution of Gothic Christians; Saba the Goth
events.summary: After the war with Valens, Athanaric persecuted Christians among the Tervingi, seeing them as a Roman fifth column; the Passion of Saba the Goth describes a village protecting its Christians and Saba's drowning in the river Musaeus (Buzău) on 12 April 372, his relics being sent by Junius Soranus, dux of Scythia, to Basil of Caesarea.

events.title: Austuriani raids on Lepcis Magna and the Romanus affair
events.summary: Austuriani nomads ravaged the territory of Lepcis in 363-365; the comes Romanus demanded 4,000 camels before acting, and when the Tripolitanians complained to Valentinian, Romanus' relative, the master of offices Remigius, ensured the envoys were punished and some executed, a scandal Ammianus narrates in detail.
